New machine. Its objects are: vesoso, mekukil, kanago, denasa, gumusu, vinatir.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: vesoso, mekukil, kanago
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first three objects did not light the machine, but I don't yet know the rule: one nexiom alone might be enough, or both might be needed. Testing the other three together tells me whether the remaining group can trigger it.

TEST: denasa, gumusu, vinatir
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group did not light the machine but the second did. I'll assume the machine responds to how many nexioms are on it. If one nexiom is enough to light it, both nexioms must be among denasa, gumusu and vinatir. If both are needed, the same is true. If it lit only for exactly one nexiom, each group would hold one and both tests would have lit, so that rule is out.

That leaves three possible pairs under two possible rules. Testing denasa and gumusu together splits these well:
- **If it doesn't light:** both nexioms must be needed, and the pair is denasa–vinatir or gumusu–vinatir. One more test will settle it.
- **If it lights:** testing denasa alone and then gumusu alone will separate the four remaining cases.

TEST: denasa, gumusu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Case analysis so far:
- No nexioms were in the first test, and it stayed dark, so zero nexioms never lights the machine.
- Both nexioms are among denasa, gumusu and vinatir.
- Denasa and gumusu together lit the machine.

That leaves four possibilities:
1. One nexiom is enough, and the pair is denasa–gumusu.
2. One nexiom is enough, and the pair is denasa–vinatir.
3. One nexiom is enough, and the pair is gumusu–vinatir.
4. Both are needed, and the pair is denasa–gumusu.

Testing denasa alone splits these in half:
- **If it lights:** it is case 1 or 2. Testing vinatir alone will tell them apart.
- **If it doesn't light:** it is case 3 or 4. Testing gumusu alone will tell them apart.

TEST: denasa
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Denasa alone lit the machine, so denasa is a nexiom and one nexiom is enough to light it. That leaves two cases:
- The pair is denasa–gumusu.
- The pair is denasa–vinatir.

Testing vinatir alone settles it. If it lights, the pair is denasa–vinatir. If it stays dark, the pair is denasa–gumusu.

TEST: vinatir
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Vinatir alone stayed dark. Denasa alone lit the machine, so one nexiom is enough to light it. That means vinatir cannot be a nexiom, which leaves denasa and gumusu as the pair.

This rests on my assumption that the machine responds only to how many nexioms are on it. My tests are consistent with that, but they could not rule out every possible rule.

ANSWER: nexioms = denasa, gumusu
One last question. If only denasa were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. This was my fourth test: denasa alone lit the machine. Since the machine responds to its nexioms in a fixed way, placing denasa by itself again should give the same result.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: muvafi, bukuvis, digamok, kakubur, gukamor, vamenil.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects together to see whether this group affects the machine.

TEST: muvafi, bukuvis, digamok
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group of three did not light the machine. I don't yet know the rule: it might light when any one nexiom is present, or only when both are. Testing the other three objects together will tell me whether the nexioms could be in that group.

TEST: kakubur, gukamor, vamenil
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The machine lit for kakubur, gukamor and vamenil, but not for the first three. Whether it lights for any single nexiom or needs both, both nexioms must be among kakubur, gukamor and vamenil. That leaves three possible pairs.

Testing kakubur and gukamor together helps either way:
- **If it stays dark:** the machine must need both nexioms, because any two of the three contain at least one. The pair is then kakubur-vamenil or gukamor-vamenil, and one more test settles it.
- **If it lights:** testing vamenil alone, then kakubur alone if needed, settles it.

TEST: kakubur, gukamor
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The machine lit for kakubur and gukamor. So either it lights for any single nexiom, in which case the pair could be any two of the three, or it needs both and the pair is kakubur-gukamor.

Testing vamenil alone separates these:
- **If it stays dark:** vamenil is not a nexiom, so the pair is kakubur-gukamor.
- **If it lights:** the pair is kakubur-vamenil or gukamor-vamenil. Testing kakubur alone will settle it.

TEST: vamenil
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Both remaining rules point to the same pair:

- **If the machine lights for any single nexiom:** the first test rules out muvafi, bukuvis and digamok. Vamenil alone stayed dark, so it is not a nexiom either. That leaves kakubur and gukamor.
- **If the machine needs both nexioms:** the kakubur-gukamor test lit, so they must be the pair.
- **If it lights only for exactly one nexiom:** the first two results cannot both happen, so this rule is out.

ANSWER: nexioms = kakubur, gukamor
One last question. If only gukamor were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

I can't tell from my tests. Each test either held both kakubur and gukamor or held neither, so I never saw one of them on its own. Two rules fit every result:

- **The machine lights when any nexiom is present:** gukamor alone would light it.
- **The machine needs both nexioms:** gukamor alone would not light it.

My results don't favour either rule, so this answer is a guess. I lean slightly towards "any nexiom", which would mean gukamor alone lights it up.

PROBE: yes

Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Sukoren is a nexiom and lights the machine on its own. Under the simple rule "lights if any nexiom is present", nifugi staying dark means the second nexiom is meposik. TEST: meposik
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Meposik lit up on its own, like sukoren. Nifugi stayed dark alone, and mubupul, limurus and fokipen stayed dark together. Every result fits the rule "lights if any nexiom is present", with sukoren and meposik as the nexioms.

One last question. If only meposik were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. My last test was exactly this, meposik alone on the machine, and it lit up. The machine responds to its nexioms in a fixed way, so the same setup should give the same result.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: tegofa, gizapas, rivoda, rasemen, norupen, ditilu.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to see how the machine reacts.

TEST: tegofa, gizapas, rivoda
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first three (tegofa, gizapas, rivoda) did not light the machine, but I don't yet know the machine's rule. If any single nexiom lights it, both nexioms must be among rasemen, norupen and ditilu. If it needs both present, the first group simply didn't contain both. Testing a pair from the remaining three will help separate these cases.

TEST: rasemen, norupen
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first test (tegofa, gizapas, rivoda) did not light up. The second (rasemen, norupen) did.

I'm considering three possible rules:
- **Either nexiom is enough:** neither nexiom is in the first group. So both are among rasemen, norupen and ditilu, and at least one is rasemen or norupen.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** the nexioms must be rasemen and norupen.
- **Exactly one nexiom is needed:** the first group can't hold both, or rasemen and norupen would hold neither. So exactly one of rasemen and norupen is a nexiom, and ditilu is the other.

Testing ditilu alone separates these cases:
- If it stays dark, the nexioms are rasemen and norupen under either of the first two rules.
- If it lights, ditilu is a nexiom. Testing rasemen alone next would then tell me whether its partner is rasemen or norupen.

TEST: ditilu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Ditilu lit up on its own, so ditilu is a nexiom and one nexiom is enough to light the machine. That rules out the "both needed" rule.

The first group (tegofa, gizapas, rivoda) could not have held a nexiom. It could not have held both either, because then rasemen and norupen would hold none, and they did light up. So the second nexiom is rasemen or norupen. Testing rasemen alone will tell me which.

TEST: rasemen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Ditilu lit the machine on its own, so one nexiom is enough. Rasemen alone stayed dark, so rasemen is not a nexiom. Since rasemen and norupen together lit up, norupen must be the second nexiom. I'll use my last test to check norupen alone.

TEST: norupen
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Norupen lit the machine on its own, which confirms it as the second nexiom. Ditilu also lit up alone, while rasemen alone did not. All five results fit a machine that lights when at least one nexiom is present, with ditilu and norupen as the nexioms:
- tegofa, gizapas, rivoda: no nexioms, stayed dark
- rasemen, norupen: norupen present, lit
- ditilu alone: lit
- rasemen alone: no nexiom, stayed dark
- norupen alone: lit

ANSWER: nexioms = ditilu, norupen
One last question. If only ditilu were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. This was directly observed, not just inferred: in my third test I placed ditilu alone on the machine and it lit up. That fits the rule that any single nexiom is enough to light the machine.

PROBE: yes
